title: The Tokens Strike Back: Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision

paper.title: The Tokens Strike Back: Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision
paper.abstract:
Abstract The Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) is a recent, training-free, safety-guidance framework for text diffusion models. During inference, SAD steers text samples toward safe regions of the token probability space.
In this paper, we propose SADDER (Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision) , which improves the safety and quality trade-offs of SAD by exploiting a safety-guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space for each token position, then updating the token positions using the SAD update rule multiplied by the guidance signal.
This multiplication acts as a gating mechanism: tokens with a high unsafe signal are more likely to be modified during inference following the SAD update rule.
However, such an update does not automatically preserve the conditional mean, i.e., the denoiser of a fixed target distribution.
We therefore theoretically derive new position-wise target distributions for which the modified denoiser is exact. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which the position-wise target distributions match a global target distribution.
We test our SADDER method on popular Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs) across unsafe continuation and jailbreak settings, and show that SADDER achieves a better balance between safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of domains, including images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , speech ( Popov et al., 2021 ) , and protein structure generation ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . In language modeling, however, autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs) remain the dominant approach, demonstrating strong capabilities in language generation and understanding, mathematical reasoning ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and coding ( Li et al., 2023 ) . Despite their success, AR models generate text one token at a time, which inherently limits inference parallelism and makes revising previously generated content less natural. Recent advances in Text Diffusion Models (TDMs) offer an alternative paradigm, in which text is generated through an iterative denoising process that can update multiple token positions and progressively refine the generated sequence ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, at comparable model scales, recent TDMs have also shown competitive performance with AR-LLMs across benchmarks; For instance, Stable-DiffCoder-8B ( Fan et al., 2026 ) vs. Seed-Coder-8B ( ByteDance Seed et al., 2025 ) on code generation benchmarks, and LLaDA-8B ( Nie et al., 2025 ) vs. LLaMA3-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) on mathematical reasoning tasks. Despite these advantages, the safety of TDMs remains relatively underexplored compared to AR-LLMs, particularly with respect to toxic content generation and vulnerability to jailbreak attacks. Traditional safety mechanisms rely on fine-tuning and alignment ( Dai et al., 2024 ) , post-hoc filtering and rejection sampling ( Naveed et al., 2025 ) , or inference-time methods that modify the decoding strategy during next-token prediction ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . However, these approaches either require additional training or assume AR decoding and therefore do not directly generalize to TDMs. Recent work has begun exploring inference-time mechanisms specifically designed for TDMs, including particle-based steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , classifier-based guidance ( Schiff et al., 2025 ) , and safety-oriented remasking approaches ( Lee and Han, 2026 ) . In particular, the Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) ( Yusuf et al., 2026 ) provides a training-free framework to steer the denoising trajectory towards a safe region in the data distribution using only a small set of 500 ∼ 1000 500\sim 1000 unsafe reference samples. Nevertheless, SAD operates in token probability space, leaving open whether semantically richer model representations could enable more effective, position-specific safety guidance. In this work, we propose SADDER ( S afety- A ware D enoising with D irectional E mbedding-based R evision), a safety-guidance method that augments SAD with position-wise signals extracted from the model’s embedding space. At each denoising step, we first identify potentially unsafe token positions based on a safety-guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space. We then use this information in a second step to modulate the SAD update, enabling more precise, position-by-position interventions along the sampling trajectory. By selectively modifying fewer positions, SADDER achieves a better balance between safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods, when tested on popular Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs) across unsafe continuation and jailbreak settings.

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: We first describe two ingredients our method builds on: masked and uniform-state TDMs in Section 2.1 , whose samplers differ in whether a committed token can still be changed in the subsequent denoising steps; and SAD in Section 2.2 , the inference-time guidance framework that our method extends.

sections.heading: 2.2 The Safety-Aware Denoiser
sections.text: The safety-aware denoiser (SAD) ( Yusuf et al., 2026 ) is a training-free guidance method that steers a pretrained TDM away from a negation set of sequences that should not be generated. It adapts the safe denoiser of Kim et al. (2025) , later extended to flow matching ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , by replacing the Gaussian corruption kernel with the categorical kernels equation 1 and equation 4 .

sections.heading: 3 Methods: SADDER
sections.text: SAD provides safety guidance in the token probability space. We can enhance this guidance by selecting a guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space for each token position, then modifying the selected token positions using the SAD update rule. In what follows, we introduce SADDER (Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision), consisting of two phases.

sections.heading: Activation steering and remasking.
sections.text: Contrastive Activation Addition ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) steers language models using directions extracted from paired examples; ILRR ( Avrahami and Nachmani, 2026 ) guides masked diffusion by aligning activations with a reference sequence. For safety, DiffuGuard ( Li et al., 2025 ) combines stochastic remasking with block-level audit and repair. Most closely related, Lee and Han (2026) construct paired samples ( x i , y i harm , y i safe ) (x_{i},y_{i}^{\mathrm{harm}},y_{i}^{\mathrm{safe}}) , using harmful model responses to WildJailbreak prompts ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) and paraphrased refusals. They estimate a Contrastive Safety Direction (CSD), v ℓ v_{\ell} , from the difference between the mean harmful and safe response representations. In Phase 1 , they modify hidden states at masked and prompt positions during the first fraction ρ \rho of the denoising steps: 𝒮 ⁡ ( h ℓ , j ( t ) ) = h ℓ , j ( t ) − β ⁡ ⟨ h ℓ , j ( t ) , v ^ ℓ ⟩ ​ v ^ ℓ , \mathcal{S}(h_{\ell,j}^{(t)})=h_{\ell,j}^{(t)}-\beta\,\langle h_{\ell,j}^{(t)},\hat{v}_{\ell}\rangle\hat{v}_{\ell}, where v ^ ℓ \hat{v}_{\ell} is the normalized CSD and β \beta controls the intervention strength. In Phase 2 , they refine the generated sequence by selecting positions according to m j ( k ) = { ⟨ h ℓ , j ( k ) , v ^ ℓ ⟩ > θ } , m_{j}^{(k)}=\mathbbm{1}\!\left\{\langle h_{\ell,j}^{(k)},\hat{v}_{\ell}\rangle>\theta\right\}, then remasking and regenerating those positions for up to K K refinement iterations, stopping early if no positions exceed the threshold. SADDER uses a similar contrastive direction, but centers the activation score at the midpoint of the harmful and safe representations. This places the zero-score boundary at their Euclidean bisector. The score gates SAD’s correction in token probability space rather than directly modifying hidden states; in masked models, it also ranks revealed positions for budgeted remasking within the denoising loop.

sections.heading: Sampling-based baselines.
sections.text: Best-of- N N sampling generates independent candidate completions and selects the one with the highest reward. FK steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) instead maintains multiple diffusion trajectories and resamples them at intermediate steps using reward-derived potentials. Both provide inference-time control without retraining the generator. SADDER modifies token predictions within each trajectory, using unsafe references and activation scores rather than ranking candidate sequences. Comparisons with Best-of- N N and FK steering assess whether this local intervention offers a better safety–quality tradeoff at a given inference budget.

sections.heading: Diffusion-specific jailbreaks.
sections.text: DIJA ( Wen et al., 2026 ) constructs interleaved text–mask prompts that exploit bidirectional context and parallel decoding to elicit harmful completions. PAD ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) adapts affirmative-response priming to parallel generation through a multi-point attention attack. These attacks expose vulnerabilities associated with diffusion’s generation process and motivate evaluating safety guidance on adversarially structured inputs as well as ordinary unsafe continuation. We include all in our evaluation of selective guidance and token revision.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We ask whether selective guidance improves the safety–quality tradeoff of SAD, and whether its benefits transfer from unsafe continuation to adversarial instructions. Following Yusuf et al. (2026) , we evaluate these tasks separately. The main continuation results distinguish SADDER from SADDER with a full-SAD warm-up. Other variants, calibration sweeps, and the extended algorithm are reported in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Safety–quality tradeoffs.
sections.text: On LLaDA/RTP, SADDER lowers the unsafe rate from 38.6% unmodified to 29.4%, versus 32.4% for full SAD; warm-up reaches 31.2%. On BeaverTails, SADDER reaches 29.9%, full SAD 27.1%, and warm-up 24.4%. Across all four model/dataset settings, SADDER achieves higher benign BERTScore and lower benign PPL than full SAD. SADDER also achieves higher benign BERTScore than warm-up throughout, although both variants remain below unmodified sampling on this metric (Tables 1 and 9 ). Harmful-prompt PPL reveals a different tradeoff: on LLaDA/RTP, CSD reaches a 22.4% unsafe rate but PPL 225, versus 42.1 for SADDER and 31.6 for warm-up without remasking. CSD’s benign PPL of 21.6 does not expose this deterioration on harmful prompts. Gains also depend on the model: on Dream, full SAD at η = 10,000 \eta=10{,}000 achieves lower unsafe rates than either SADDER variant on both datasets. BoN-8 further reduces unsafe rates at a cost of 256 generator evaluations plus reward scoring.

Large HB reductions from CSD and full-block DiffuGuard do not yield comparable LG reductions: Dream’s full-block DiffuGuard reaches 33.3% HB ASR but 84.0% LG unsafe rate and PPL 537. Both judges assess complete responses, so this discrepancy cannot be attributed solely to scaffold inclusion. Appendix H.5 separates evaluator choice from the influence of fixed attack text by comparing full-response and generated-span judgments on the same outputs. SADDER retains generator cost and incurs a smaller PPL increase, but offers limited DIJA robustness. PAD gives a more favorable result: Dream warm-up reduces HB ASR by 9.0 points (paired 95% CI: [ − 15.7 , − 2.3 ] [-15.7,-2.3] ), lowers LG unsafe rate from 64.0% to 55.0%, and increases PPL from 8.53 to 10.40. This supports an attack-specific tradeoff rather than general jailbreak robustness. Appendix H reports component, strength, and timing studies.

sections.heading: Over-refusal.
sections.text: Dream warm-up reduces WG refusal on safe XSTest prompts by 35.4 points on jointly scored outputs (95% CI: [ − 41.6 , − 29.3 ] [-41.6,-29.3] ), but raises WG harmfulness on unsafe contrasts from 0.0% to 6.9% among scored responses. Fewer refusals therefore do not establish greater helpfulness at unchanged safety.

sections.heading: 6 Summary and Discussion
sections.text: We introduced SADDER, an extension of the Safety-Aware Denoiser, using midpoint-centred contrastive activation scores to select where to apply probability-space safety guidance. Rather than directly modifying hidden representations, SADDER uses them to identify potentially risky positions and applies the SAD correction to the corresponding token distributions. Our theoretical analysis characterizes the conditions under which position-wise guidance recovers the conditional mean of an induced safe target, and identifies when these local conditional means agree with a global target. Experiments on masked and uniform-state diffusion models reveal both the benefits and limitations of selective guidance. SADDER improves benign-continuation quality metrics relative to full SAD in several settings, with selected configurations also reducing unsafe generation. Jailbreak improvements also depend on the model and operating point, but SADDER shows significantly lower refusal rates. Taken together, SADDER offers an additional way to manage the safety–quality and safety-refusal trade-offs.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work investigates training-free safety guidance for text diffusion models. Our experiments involve toxic text, harmful instructions, and adversarial prompts from existing datasets and benchmarks. These materials serve a defensive evaluation purpose but may contain offensive or distressing content. Analysis of model vulnerabilities could also inform attempts to circumvent safeguards. Any release of associated harmful generations or attack artifacts should therefore consider risks of misuse, exposure to harmful content, and disclosure of sensitive information. Furthermore, safety guidance could be misused to suppress legitimate expression, while overly broad or biased safety criteria may restrict benign content and disproportionately affect particular communities. Our evaluation relies on benchmark datasets and automated safety judges, which may reflect social biases and fail to capture context-dependent harms. Differences between evaluators further limit the interpretation of reported safety metrics. We report safety alongside generation quality, inference cost, and over-refusal, including settings where the proposed guidance offers limited benefit. Reduced refusal does not necessarily imply improved helpfulness, and lower measured attack success does not establish that responses are safe or usable. Our findings are restricted to the evaluated models, datasets, and sampling configurations; they do not establish safety across untested settings. Deployment would require additional assessment of robustness, fairness, and risks specific to the intended application.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The main text presents the mathematical formulation of SADDER, and Algorithm 1 specifies the selective guidance procedure. Appendix A.2 derives the centered-score equivalence, and Appendices A.4 and A.5 provide proofs of the theoretical results. Appendix A.6 describes the datasets, prompt selection, and reference-set construction. Appendix A.8 documents shared settings, hyperparameter ranges, and configuration selection, while Appendix B details the sampling extensions. Appendices E and H report additional experimental settings and results. Appendix H.5 compares evaluators and response scopes, and Appendix H.2 describes refusal evaluation and the handling of missing judge labels. Appendix B.2 specifies metric aggregation, seed standard deviations, bootstrap intervals, and paired comparisons. These materials support independent implementation and assessment of the reported results.

sections.heading: A.6 Datasets, prompt selection, and reference construction
sections.text: We distinguish three data roles: evaluation prompts, unsafe references for the SAD update, and safe/harmful examples for constructing the activation direction. A benchmark used for one role is not automatically used for the others.

sections.heading: RealToxicityPrompts (RTP).
sections.text: RTP contains naturally occurring text prefixes and their original continuations, with Perspective annotations ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) . For unsafe continuation, the configured pool requires a maximum available prompt-side Perspective score of at least 0.8 and a subsequent Llama-Guard unsafe verdict on the prompt. Its builder also retains the adapter’s continuation-score floor of 0.5. These filters describe an enriched evaluation cohort, not the full RTP distribution. Since Llama-Guard also judges generated outputs, the prompt selection is not judge-independent. Note the negation set used to construct the unsafe reference bank for the contrastive direction is not Llama-Guard scored. The original RTP development/search set comprises pool indices 0–299. The reported continuation tables use the expanded evaluation set, indices 300–899, collected as three 200-prompt shards at offsets 300, 500, and 700. These evaluation records exclude the original development records. The subsequent configuration-selection procedure is described below.

sections.heading: BeaverTails.
sections.text: BeaverTails provides instruction–response pairs with response-safety annotations ( Ji et al., 2023 ) . We condition on prompts associated with unsafe-labeled responses, using 600 records for the evaluation set. The corresponding unsafe responses supply the negative reference set and safe-labeled responses supply the safe direction set. An unsafe response annotation does not establish that its prompt is itself malicious.

sections.heading: Benign continuation controls.
sections.text: The quality cohort requires both the maximum prompt-side Perspective score and the maximum score from the continuation’s own fields to be at most 0.2. We remove duplicate prompt strings and prompt strings present in the excluded unsafe-reference artifacts, shuffle with seed zero, and retain 600 records. BERTScore compares each generated response with its own benign human continuation, including for unmodified sampling. BeaverTails-tuned methods use this same benign RTP cohort while retaining their BeaverTails reference banks. This is a quality diagnostic rather than an independent capability evaluation.

sections.heading: JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and HarmBench.
sections.text: JailbreakBench supplies harmful behaviors for standardized jailbreak evaluation ( Chao et al., 2024 ) ; its 100 harmful behaviors are development data in our study. AdvBench contains harmful instructions used to evaluate adversarial prompting ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . HarmBench provides harmful behaviors and a behavior-conditioned evaluation classifier ( Mazeika et al., 2024a ) and our jobs restrict evaluation to its standard behavior category. We shuffle with seed zero and use the first 100 behaviors of each dataset for development. The transfer protocol reserves AdvBench offsets 100–519 and HarmBench-standard offsets 100–199. The main jailbreak tables report the latter held-out HarmBench cohort under DIJA and PAD. These are our experimental splits, not official benchmark train/test partitions.

sections.heading: WildJailbreak and the jailbreak reference bank.
sections.text: WildJailbreak contains both harmful and benign prompts, including adversarial rewrites ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) . Our unsafe set construction selects the adversarial-harmful training subset, skips the first 1,000 filtered records, and generates LLaDA-Instruct responses from three disjoint 1,300-prompt windows. Exact evaluation-behavior strings are excluded. Generation uses 256 steps, up to 256 new tokens, temperature zero, and seed 42. Unsafe-response filtering, refusal filtering, and deduplication produce the documented 357-response unsafe WildJailbreak set. The jailbreak contrastive direction uses unsafe responses and refusal references with the chat template and a 64-token response cap.

sections.heading: XSTest and over-refusal.
sections.text: XSTest contains 250 safe prompts that models should answer and 200 unsafe contrast prompts ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) . Over-refusal is the refusal rate on the safe subset, reported separately from refusal on unsafe prompts. Our runs use unmodified prompts through the model’s chat template ( vanilla ). The evaluator we use matches the response opening against XSTest’s full-refusal strings; it does not detect partial refusals or every paraphrased refusal.

sections.heading: A.7 Models, attacks, and evaluation measures
sections.text: We use LLaDA-8B-Base and LLaDA-8B-Instruct ( Nie et al., 2025 ) , and Dream-7B-Base and Dream-7B-Instruct ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . The base checkpoints are evaluated by prompted continuation; instruction checkpoints use the attack-specific input construction. The implementation’s layer k k follows the hidden-state indexing and interior layers are inputs to block k k , and the final layer includes the model’s final normalization.

sections.heading: Attacks and fixed context.
sections.text: Zero-shot runs present the original harmful behavior through the chat template. DIJA fills mask spans inside the saved adversarial prompt ( Wen et al., 2026 ) and the refined prompts are reused across methods. PAD inserts fixed anchors into the generation region ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . SADDER and generation-scope DiffuGuard modify only initially editable positions. Full-block DiffuGuard additionally permits repair of fixed scaffold text after the first masked position, including PAD anchors; under DIJA it also appends the released implementation’s extra masked tail. The main jailbreak tables concern DIJA and PAD.

sections.heading: Safety and quality.
sections.text: Llama-Guard-3-8B ( Meta, 2024 ) judges the generated response alone under continuation framing. HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls ( Mazeika et al., 2024a ; Mazeika et al., 2024b ) judges the response against the requested behavior. We report their respective unsafe rates separately. GPT-2-large ( Radford et al., 2019 ) scores generated text with a causal language-model likelihood; this is an external fluency proxy for both model families, not LLaDA’s pseudo-perplexity. Padding and text after the first end-of-sequence token are excluded. Harmful PPL includes all scorable outputs on the unsafe cohort, whether the safety judge labels them safe or unsafe. Benign PPL and BERTScore F1 ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) use the separate benign cohort. BERTScore specifies English and disables baseline rescaling; it leaves the encoder to the installed package’s default. BERTScore is multiplied by 100 in the tables. Higher reference similarity and lower PPL are useful diagnostics, but neither alone establishes helpfulness or safety.

sections.heading: WildGuard response views.
sections.text: For DIJA, the appendix additionally reports WildGuard Han et al. (2024) harmfulness on the newline-joined spans marked as initially masked, paired with the original harmful behavior. This excludes the fixed scaffold and any full-block repairs outside those spans. Full-response WildGuard harmfulness and refusal remain in the appendix; XSTest uses full-response refusal. The generated-span evaluation is available only for fixed-policy DIJA runs, not PAD or the window studies (Appendix H.5 ).

sections.heading: Uncertainty and cost.
sections.text: Tables report averages with 95% confidence intervals, estimated by repeatedly resampling the evaluation prompts. The appendix also reports standard deviations (SDs) across three generation seeds, showing how much results vary between runs. Appendix B.2 explains both measures and the paired comparisons. NFE counts generator forward passes, including additional passes after remasking. It excludes reward scoring, safety judges, and preparation of the reference set, so it measures generator computation rather than total runtime.

sections.heading: Motivation for remasking.
sections.text: The safety improvements reported by CSD-based steering and DiffuGuard ( Lee and Han, 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) motivate examining remasking as an optional extension to SADDER. Reopening previously generated positions allows guidance to revise token choices that would otherwise remain fixed. Uniform-state diffusion provides a related capability through its native token replacement transitions, allowing repeated revision without an explicit mask token. As such, we wanted to evaluate selective SAD with risk-based remasking and matched random controls in the appendix.

B.2 Metric estimates and uncertainty
sections.text: We compute uncertainty from the saved evaluations. Let i = 1 , … , n i=1,\ldots,n index evaluation records and s = 1 , … , S s=1,\ldots,S index the observed generation seeds. The main continuation evaluations have n = 600 n=600 and S = 3 S=3 ; the main HarmBench evaluations have n = 100 n=100 and S = 3 S=3 .

sections.heading: Unsafe rates and other averages.
sections.text: Let y i , s ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i,s}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the output for prompt record i i and seed s s is judged unsafe. On a complete, balanced evaluation, the unsafe percentage is r ^ unsafe = 100 n ​ S ​ ∑ i = 1 n ∑ s = 1 S y i , s . \widehat{r}_{\mathrm{unsafe}}=\frac{100}{nS}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{s=1}^{S}y_{i,s}. (55) The same expression defines HarmBench ASR, refusal rate, or short-output rate when y i , s y_{i,s} is the corresponding event indicator. A mean repetition score uses the per-output repetition score instead. Each metric retains its own evaluation population: for example, XSTest over-refusal uses only safe prompts. When observation counts differ, rate estimates use the total number of valid observations as their denominator.

sections.heading: Quality metrics.
sections.text: Let ℐ s \mathcal{I}_{s} contain the valid records for a quality metric at seed s s . The reported mean averages a metric computed within each seed: Q ^ s = f ⁡ ( ∑ i ∈ ℐ s A i , s ∑ i ∈ ℐ s D i , s ) , Q ^ = 1 S ​ ∑ s = 1 S Q ^ s . \widehat{Q}_{s}=f\!\left(\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{s}}A_{i,s}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{s}}D_{i,s}}\right),\qquad\widehat{Q}=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\widehat{Q}_{s}. (56) For BERTScore, A i , s A_{i,s} is the response-level F1 score, D i , s = 1 D_{i,s}=1 , and f ⁡ ( z ) = z f(z)=z ; the displayed values are multiplied by 100. For PPL, A i , s A_{i,s} is the total negative log likelihood of scored tokens, D i , s D_{i,s} is their count, and f ⁡ ( z ) = exp ⁡ ( z ) f(z)=\exp(z) . Thus PPL is an average of seed-level corpus perplexities, not an average of response perplexities. Missing or unscorable measurements are excluded; they are not assigned zero.

sections.heading: 95% confidence intervals.
sections.text: To estimate uncertainty due to the evaluation prompts, we randomly sample prompts from the evaluated set, allowing the same prompt to be selected more than once. Each resampled set has the same number of prompts as the original set. Whenever a prompt is selected, we keep its responses from all three seeds together. We calculate the metric again for each resampled set and repeat this process 5,000 times. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of these 5,000 estimates form the reported 95% confidence interval.

sections.text: For seed-level estimates θ ^ s \widehat{\theta}_{s} , the reported sample SD is SD seed = 1 S − 1 ​ ∑ s = 1 S ( θ ^ s − θ ¯ seed ) 2 , θ ¯ seed = 1 S ​ ∑ s θ ^ s . \operatorname{SD}_{\mathrm{seed}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{S-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}(\widehat{\theta}_{s}-\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{seed}})^{2}},\qquad\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{seed}}=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s}\widehat{\theta}_{s}. (57) It describes variation across runs and is not a confidence interval; it is unavailable for a single seed. sections.heading: Refusal detection and coverage.
sections.text: The detectors assign different refusal rates to the same responses. For LLaDA warm-up on unsafe prompts, opening-string matching gives 53.5% refusal and WildGuard gives 97.5%; the corresponding Dream rates are 69.5% and 91.5%. sections.heading: Separating generated content from the attack scaffold.
sections.text: DIJA completions contain both fixed attack text and model-generated spans. A harmfulness judgment on the complete response can therefore depend on text supplied by the attacker. We compare HarmBench (HB), LlamaGuard (LG), and WildGuard (WG) on two response views: the complete response, including the scaffold, and only the spans marked as initially masked in the saved completion segmentation ( fills ). Nonempty spans are trimmed and joined by newlines before judging. HB measures behavior-specific attack success, LG unsafe content, and WG response harmfulness. These are distinct evaluator criteria, even when the response view is held fixed. The main table retains full-response HB/LG for attacks and uses WG only for XSTest. Generated-span attack scores from all three judges are reported here. All response-view comparisons use the same generated completions and defence settings, so differences between views reflect the scoring procedure. This view isolates the initially editable content, rather than judging the assembled attack response. Removing intervening text can change the context needed to interpret a span. For full-block DiffuGuard, repairs outside the initially masked spans are also excluded. Generated-span scores thus complement complete-response judgments; they do not measure the safety of every token that a defence may modify.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.17636v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2026 The Tokens Strike Back: Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision Amman Yusuf Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of British Columbia, Canada Email: ammany01@cs.ubc.ca Jiwoo Shin Affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), South Korea Ruizhi Deng Affiliation: RBC Borealis, Canada Heitor Rodrigues Guimarães Affiliation: RBC Borealis, Canada Nikita Dvornik Affiliation: RBC Borealis, Canada Mijung Park Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of British Columbia, Canada Abstract The Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) is a recent, training-free, safety-guidance framework for text diffusion models. During inference, SAD steers text samples toward safe regions of the token probability space. In this paper, we propose SADDER (Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision) , which improves the safety and quality trade-offs of SAD by exploiting a safety-guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space for each token position, then updating the token positions using the SAD update rule multiplied by the guidance signal. This multiplication acts as a gating mechanism: tokens with a high unsafe signal are more likely to be modified during inference following the SAD update rule. However, such an update does not automatically preserve the conditional mean, i.e., the denoiser of a fixed target distribution. We therefore theoretically derive new position-wise target distributions for which the modified denoiser is exact. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which the position-wise target distributions match a global target distribution. We test our SADDER method on popular Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs) across unsafe continuation and jailbreak settings, and show that SADDER achieves a better balance between safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods. 1 Introduction Diffusion models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of domains, including images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , speech ( Popov et al., 2021 ) , and protein structure generation ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . In language modeling, however, autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs) remain the dominant approach, demonstrating strong capabilities in language generation and understanding, mathematical reasoning ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and coding ( Li et al., 2023 ) . Despite their success, AR models generate text one token at a time, which inherently limits inference parallelism and makes revising previously generated content less natural. Recent advances in Text Diffusion Models (TDMs) offer an alternative paradigm, in which text is generated through an iterative denoising process that can update multiple token positions and progressively refine the generated sequence ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, at comparable model scales, recent TDMs have also shown competitive performance with AR-LLMs across benchmarks; For instance, Stable-DiffCoder-8B ( Fan et al., 2026 ) vs. Seed-Coder-8B ( ByteDance Seed et al., 2025 ) on code generation benchmarks, and LLaDA-8B ( Nie et al., 2025 ) vs. LLaMA3-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) on mathematical reasoning tasks. Despite these advantages, the safety of TDMs remains relatively underexplored compared to AR-LLMs, particularly with respect to toxic content generation and vulnerability to jailbreak attacks. Traditional safety mechanisms rely on fine-tuning and alignment ( Dai et al., 2024 ) , post-hoc filtering and rejection sampling ( Naveed et al., 2025 ) , or inference-time methods that modify the decoding strategy during next-token prediction ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . However, these approaches either require additional training or assume AR decoding and therefore do not directly generalize to TDMs. Recent work has begun exploring inference-time mechanisms specifically designed for TDMs, including particle-based steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , classifier-based guidance ( Schiff et al., 2025 ) , and safety-oriented remasking approaches ( Lee and Han, 2026 ) . In particular, the Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) ( Yusuf et al., 2026 ) provides a training-free framework to steer the denoising trajectory towards a safe region in the data distribution using only a small set of 500 ∼ 1000 500\sim 1000 unsafe reference samples. Nevertheless, SAD operates in token probability space, leaving open whether semantically richer model representations could enable more effective, position-specific safety guidance. In this work, we propose SADDER ( S afety- A ware D enoising with D irectional E mbedding-based R evision), a safety-guidance method that augments SAD with position-wise signals extracted from the model’s embedding space. At each denoising step, we first identify potentially unsafe token positions based on a safety-guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space. We then use this information in a second step to modulate the SAD update, enabling more precise, position-by-position interventions along the sampling trajectory. By selectively modifying fewer positions, SADDER achieves a better balance between safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods, when tested on popular Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs) across unsafe continuation and jailbreak settings. 2 Background We first describe two ingredients our method builds on: masked and uniform-state TDMs in Section 2.1 , whose samplers differ in whether a committed token can still be changed in the subsequent denoising steps; and SAD in Section 2.2 , the inference-time guidance framework that our method extends. 2.1 Text Diffusion Models A TDM corrupts a clean token sequence 𝒙 0 1 : L {\bm{x}}_{0}^{1:L} of length L L with a fixed forward process and learns to reverse it. Contrastive Activation Addition ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) steers language models using directions extracted from paired examples; ILRR ( Avrahami and Nachmani, 2026 ) guides masked diffusion by aligning activations with a reference sequence. For safety, DiffuGuard ( Li et al., 2025 ) combines stochastic remasking with block-level audit and repair. Most closely related, Lee and Han (2026) construct paired samples ( x i , y i harm , y i safe ) (x_{i},y_{i}^{\mathrm{harm}},y_{i}^{\mathrm{safe}}) , using harmful model responses to WildJailbreak prompts ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) and paraphrased refusals. They estimate a Contrastive Safety Direction (CSD), v ℓ v_{\ell} , from the difference between the mean harmful and safe response representations. In Phase 1 , they modify hidden states at masked and prompt positions during the first fraction ρ \rho of the denoising steps: 𝒮 ⁡ ( h ℓ , j ( t ) ) = h ℓ , j ( t ) − β ⁡ ⟨ h ℓ , j ( t ) , v ^ ℓ ⟩ ​ v ^ ℓ , \mathcal{S}(h_{\ell,j}^{(t)})=h_{\ell,j}^{(t)}-\beta\,\langle h_{\ell,j}^{(t)},\hat{v}_{\ell}\rangle\hat{v}_{\ell}, where v ^ ℓ \hat{v}_{\ell} is the normalized CSD and β \beta controls the intervention strength. In Phase 2 , they refine the generated sequence by selecting positions according to m j ( k ) = { ⟨ h ℓ , j ( k ) , v ^ ℓ ⟩ > θ } , m_{j}^{(k)}=\mathbbm{1}\!\left\{\langle h_{\ell,j}^{(k)},\hat{v}_{\ell}\rangle>\theta\right\}, then remasking and regenerating those positions for up to K K refinement iterations, stopping early if no positions exceed the threshold. SADDER uses a similar contrastive direction, but centers the activation score at the midpoint of the harmful and safe representations. This places the zero-score boundary at their Euclidean bisector. The score gates SAD’s correction in token probability space rather than directly modifying hidden states; in masked models, it also ranks revealed positions for budgeted remasking within the denoising loop. Sampling-based baselines. Best-of- N N sampling generates independent candidate completions and selects the one with the highest reward. FK steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) instead maintains multiple diffusion trajectories and resamples them at intermediate steps using reward-derived potentials. Both provide inference-time control without retraining the generator. SADDER modifies token predictions within each trajectory, using unsafe references and activation scores rather than ranking candidate sequences. Comparisons with Best-of- N N and FK steering assess whether this local intervention offers a better safety–quality tradeoff at a given inference budget. Diffusion-specific jailbreaks. DIJA ( Wen et al., 2026 ) constructs interleaved text–mask prompts that exploit bidirectional context and parallel decoding to elicit harmful completions. PAD ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) adapts affirmative-response priming to parallel generation through a multi-point attention attack. These attacks expose vulnerabilities associated with diffusion’s generation process and motivate evaluating safety guidance on adversarially structured inputs as well as ordinary unsafe continuation.
